titre: The Coase Theorem: Who Holds a Right Doesn't Decide Who Wins
accroche: In 1960, an article on the economics of law puts forward a contrarian idea: as long as people can negotiate at no cost, it doesn't matter who is given the right.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1960, the British economist Ronald Coase publishes in the Journal of Law and Economics a forty-four-page article, “The Problem of Social Cost,” that will become one of the most cited texts in the entire discipline. In it he extends an insight developed the previous year on radio frequencies: Coase had then argued that if the rights to a frequency band were clearly assigned, it did not matter that two neighboring stations interfered with each other; the operators would end up working things out between themselves.

## The Farmer and the Rancher

Coase generalizes the idea with a textbook case that has remained famous: a rancher whose cattle, with no fence, trample the neighboring farmer's wheat field. Who should pay to prevent the damage: the rancher who fences in his herd, or the farmer who fences in his field? The common intuition answers: whoever causes the harm. Coase shows that the answer does not depend on the morality of the situation but on the negotiation: if putting up a fence costs less than the lost harvest, both parties have an interest in agreeing to build it, whether the law gives the rancher the freedom to let his cattle graze wherever he likes, or gives the farmer the right to be protected. In both cases, provided negotiation costs nothing, the final result, which puts up the fence, is identical. Only who ends up paying for it changes. This is what the economist George Stigler will name, in 1966, the “Coase theorem”: the initial allocation of property rights does not determine the economic outcome, only its distribution between the parties.

## What Coase Really Meant

The irony, often pointed out, is that Coase himself wrote in 1990 that he feared his article had been largely misunderstood. His aim was not to describe a frictionless world in which law could be dispensed with, but the opposite: to show that negotiation costs are never zero in the real world (bringing the parties together, gathering information, drafting an agreement, enforcing it, all of this has a price) and that this is precisely why the allocation of property rights matters, and must be designed so that whoever holds them is encouraged to use them efficiently. The article thus shifts the debate on pollution or neighborly disputes: it invites us to compare, case by case, the real costs of each institutional arrangement (market, private contract, public regulation) rather than deciding in advance that only the law can correct harm between private parties. Coase will receive the Bank of Sweden Prize in Economic Sciences for this work in 1991, thirty-one years after its publication.

repere.texte: Published in 1960 in the Journal of Law and Economics, “The Problem of Social Cost” earns Ronald Coase the Bank of Sweden Prize in Economic Sciences in 1991. As early as 1990, thirty years after its publication, he would nonetheless write that he feared his most cited article had been largely misunderstood.

carte.punch: It doesn't matter who is given the right, as long as people can negotiate at no cost.
carte.idee: In 1960, Ronald Coase shows that between a rancher and a neighboring farmer, the efficient outcome of a dispute, which puts up the fence, is the same no matter which side is initially given the right, provided negotiation costs nothing. Only the final distribution of the cost changes.
carte.source_courte: Coase, Journal of Law and Economics, 1960

quiz.question: What does Coase really show with the example of the farmer and the rancher, according to his own retrospective judgment of the 1960 article?
choix: That the state should always arbitrate neighborhood disputes rather than let the parties negotiate
That law has no influence on economic outcomes, whatever the circumstances
That whoever causes harm must always be the one who pays for the repair
That negotiation costs are never actually zero, which makes the allocation of rights decisive
quiz.explication: Coase says he meant to show the opposite of what is often attributed to him: a world without negotiation costs does not exist, and it is precisely because these costs are real that the initial allocation of property rights matters and must be thought through carefully.

quiz_supplementaire.question: On what subject had Coase developed, in 1959, the insight that he then generalizes in 1960?
choix: Radio frequencies assigned to neighboring stations that interfere with each other
Fishing rights in British territorial waters in the 20th century
The regulation of the coal trade between France and England
Pharmaceutical patents filed by competing companies
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Coase had argued in 1959 that if the rights to a radio frequency band were clearly assigned, the operators of neighboring stations would work things out among themselves despite the interference.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who gave the Coase theorem its name, and when?
choix: Ronald Coase himself, in the 1960 article he devoted to this theorem
George Stigler, in 1966, six years after the article was published
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, at the 1991 Nobel Prize
John Locke, as early as the 17th century, in an economic treatise
quiz_supplementaire.explication: It is the economist George Stigler who named the idea the “Coase theorem” in 1966, six years after the publication of Coase's article in the Journal of Law and Economics.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In the farmer and rancher example, what stays the same no matter which party is given the right, if negotiation costs nothing?
choix: Who ends up paying to put up the fence
The total wheat harvest produced by the farmer
The final outcome: who actually puts up the fence between the two plots
The number of cattle the rancher is entitled to own
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Coase shows that the final outcome, namely who puts up the fence when it costs less than the lost harvest, stays the same; only who pays for it changes.
